I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 14:00 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T21:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 63.367 degrees and its azimuth is 206.962 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 50.94 degrees and its azimuth is 157.604 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.95 percent illuminated, 28.172 degrees from the Sun, and 371351.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not reliably, despite the Moon being well above the horizon.

At 5.95% illumination and only 28.2° from the Sun, this is a very thin waxing crescent in bright afternoon daylight. Its altitude of about 51° is favorable, and clear skies help, but the close solar elongation is the main problem: the surrounding sky will be extremely bright and the crescent’s surface brightness/contrast will be very low.

For an ordinary unaided observer, even one who knows the approximate location, it would be a difficult-to-impossible naked-eye target at 14:00 PDT. A highly experienced observer might occasionally pick it out with careful shielding of the Sun and very transparent sky, but it would not be something to count on—and searching near the Sun carries an eye-safety risk.

If you try:

- **Do not look toward the Sun through binoculars, a telescope, camera viewfinder, or any optical aid.**
- Physically block the Sun with a building, roof edge, tree trunk, or your hand held well away from your line of sight.
- The Moon is about **28° east/left of the Sun** in the sky at that moment (azimuth ~158° versus Sun ~207°), and somewhat lower: roughly a few fist-widths to the left and down when facing the Sun’s general direction.
- It may become substantially easier later in the afternoon as the Sun drops and the sky darkens somewhat—though the Moon will also descend.

So: **geometrically it is up, but visually it is an exceptionally challenging daylight crescent; most people would not spot it unaided at that time.**
